statements.claim: Dwaraka sent its warriors to war with music: conch-shells and bugles sounded, bards sang, and crowds shouted victory-blessings as Krishna made ready to leave.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'with the sound of conch-shells and bugles, the songs of bards and panegyrists by thousands and blessings of men exclaiming victory Janarddana appeared like the moon, sun and Sakra.'

statements.claim: Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson and the young son of Pradyumna, had been carried off to the city of the demon Bana and lay captive there, and the Yadava chiefs had resolved to bring him home.
statements.evidence: Pack index/summary: 'To rescue Aniruddha from Bana...'; 1.268 lament: 'who has stolen away his heroic grandson Aniruddha'; the 1.268 excerpt merged with 1.264 per the pack's own audit note (same departure beat for the Bana-war rescue).

statements.claim: Instead of chariots or armies Krishna thought of Garuda in his mind, and the bird arrived at once; the son of Vinata rose into the sky and his beauty, touched by the radiance of his rider, became immense.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 excerpt: 'Govinda thought of Garuda in his mind: and he too, with folded hands, arrived before Krishna... Krishna sat on his back'; 1.264: 'when Vinatā's son flew up into the sky his beauty, increased by Hari's energy, became immense.'

statements.claim: Desiring to kill Bana, Krishna assumed a form with eight arms, towering like a mountain, crowned with innumerable heads; right hands held sword, discus, club and arrows; left hands the shield (leathern protector), Sharanga bow, thunderbolt and conch.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'Desirous of killing Vāna the lotus-eyed Keshava assumed a form having eight arms and resembling a mountain... assumed innumerable heads. In his four right hands he had sword, discus, club and arrows and by his left four hands he held the leathern protector, the Srānga-bow, the thunder-bolt and conch-shell.'

statements.claim: Balarama sat behind Krishna on Garuda, holding a thousand forms, white-armed and white-weaponed, shining like the rising moon over Mount Kailasa.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'Seated on Garudha's back, Sanghkarshana, holding a thousand forms and white weapons... like the mount Kailāsha... shone like the rising moon.'

statements.claim: Pradyumna, eager to display his prowess in battle, took a form radiant as the sage Sanatkumara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'With a view to display his prowess in battle the high-souled Pradyumna assumed a form like that of Sanatkumār.'

statements.claim: Garuda's wingbeats shook innumerable mountains and checked the wind, and with the speed of the mind he crossed the sacred path of the Siddhas and Charanas.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'shaking innumerable mountains and obstructing the course of the wind... Endued with the speed of the mind he crossed the most sacred route of the Siddhas and Chāranas.'

statements.claim: Balarama asked why they had suddenly lost their radiance and turned golden, wondering if they had come to Mount Sumeru; Krishna answered that Bana's city was near, that a fire blazing out of it to protect it had cast its glow on them, and that the effulgence of the fire of oblation had changed their colour.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264 (dialogue verses 9-15) matches nearly verbatim, including 'Have we come to the side of the mount Sumeru?' and 'we have been possessed by the effulgence of the fire of oblation: this has changed our colour.'

statements.claim: Balarama said that if approaching Bana's city cost them their lustre, Krishna should do what he thought proper afterwards; Krishna told Garuda, 'Son of Vinata, do what you think proper. When you have found a way, I will do what is proper.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264 verses 13-16: Rāma's reply and 'The Lord said:—O Vinatā's son, do what you think proper. After you have found out a means I shall do what I think proper.'

statements.claim: Garuda assumed a thousand mouths, drank from the celestial Ganga, showered its water on the city's fire and extinguished it, and was astonished that the fire had changed even Krishna's colour.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264 verses 17-18: Garuda 'assumed a thousand mouths... went to the etherial Gangā... shower it on the fire... the fire was at once extinguished... Oh! How powerful is this fire... It disfigured the color of even the intelligent Krishna.'

statements.claim: The fire-gods, followers of Rudra, saw three dreadful men of many forms riding Garuda, wondered who they were, and attacked; a great uproar arose as they and their armies fought the three Yadus.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'Seeing them the fires, the followers of Rudra, thought:—Who are these three dreadful men... They then began to fight with the three Yadus. A great noise arose...'

statements.claim: The chief of the fires, Angira, ascended a blazing chariot and lifted his mace; Krishna warned the fire-gods their destruction was near; Angira rushed with a burning trident; Krishna cut down his mace with crescent arrows, struck his breast with a death-like arrow, and Angira fell bathed in blood; the other fire-gods, sons of Brahma, fled toward Bana's city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: 'Ascending a fiery car the great saint Angirā, uplifting his effulgent mace, was shining... cutting off his mace with crescent-shaped and sharpened arrows... struck Angirā on the breast with a death-like-arrow. Thereat Angirā fell down bathed in blood... the four fire-gods, the sons of Brahmā... speedily fled away to Vāna's city.'

statements.claim: The towers of Sonitpura (Bana's city, where Aniruddha lay captive) rose into view at the flight's end.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264 concludes with 'seeing Vāna's city from a distance Nārada said...'; the pack title and summary identify Vana's city as Sonitpura.

notes: Clean rendering of HV 1.264 with the 1.268 Garuda-summoning excerpt merged for the same departure beat (per the pack's own audit note). Only liberties are atmospheric ('wings folded, waiting' for the source's 'with folded hands', 'halfway across the world', 'the sky seeming to part') — connective narration, no unsupported facts.

statements.claim: Aniruddha's wives and their companions wept in his empty rooms like ewes (crying for a lost lamb), lamenting that even under Krishna's protection they grieved, that the hero whose arms sheltered the gods had had his grandson stolen, and that they were brought under the sway of death.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 verses 1-8: 'his beloved wives and their companions cried there in his absence, like so many ewes... Alas! even under the protection of the Lord Krishna, we are weeping helplessly... who has stolen away his heroic grandson Aniruddha... we have been brought under control by death.'

statements.claim: Their cries rose like the noise of thousands of ospreys, and the whole city heard.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.11-12: 'The cries of those women in the palace set up a noise like that of thousands of female ospreys crying in the sky.' ('the whole city heard' = connective.)

statements.claim: The Yadu chiefs rushed out of their houses like lions from caves, asking whence the fear came and why such noise was heard in Aniruddha's house; the great bugle of Krishna's court was sounded, the Yadavas assembled, asked one another what had happened, and answered as they had heard.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.13-17: 'the Yadu chiefs all on sudden leaped down from their respective houses. As the lions... so the Yadavas... said... Whence is then this fear? Why is such a noise heard in Aniruddha's house? Thereupon the huge bugle of Krishna's court was brought and sounded...'

statements.claim: The eyes of the Yadavas, reddened in anger, filled with tears, and they sat sighing helplessly.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.18: 'the eyes, reddened in anger, of the Yadavas dreadful in battle, were filled with tears; and they sighed there idly.'

statements.claim: Viprithu alone spoke, urging Krishna — who sat sighing again and again — to explain his anxiety, noting the Yadavas ranged free under his protection and that even Indra slept happily leaving success and defeat to him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.19-25: Viprithu's speech, including 'even the powerful Sakra is sleeping happily' and 'Why do you not speak any thing?'

statements.claim: Krishna answered that he had been anxiously thinking without being able to settle anything; that because of Aniruddha's captivity all kings and friends would consider him incapable; that formerly king Ahuka had been taken captive by Shalwa and brought back after a dreadful fight, and that Rukmini's son Pradyumna, stolen by Shamvara in infancy, had slain him and come back.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.26-31: 'Formerly our king Ahuka was taken captive by Shālwa—but we brought him back after a dreadful fight. Rukshmini's son Pradyumna was stolen away by Shamvara in his infancy. But he, having slain him in battle, has come back.'

statements.claim: Krishna said he would kill in battle, with all his people, the one who had set an ash-covered foot upon his head.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.31: 'I will in battle kill him with his own people who has put on my head this foot covered with ashes.'

statements.claim: Satyaki advised despatching spies over the earth with its mountains and forests, engaging open and secret emissaries.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.32-34: 'despatch spies all over for finding out Aniruddha. Let them search the earth with mountains and forests. Let open and secret emissaries be engaged in this work.'

statements.claim: King Ahuka ordered messengers to search all countries lying on and under the earth, gave them horses and chariots, and told them to search the mountains Rikshavan and Raivataka, the gardens, forests, creeks and corners, riding on horses and elephants.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 v.35-39: 'Search out all the countries lying on and under the earth'... 'search the mountains Rikshavān and Raivataka'... 'Riding on horses and elephants do you soon find out Aniruddha.'

statements.claim: The messengers returned having found nothing, saying 'We saw Aniruddha nowhere.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 pack excerpt: '...the messengers... said:—...we saw Aniruddha nowhere.' (The printed passage is truncated before this point, but the pack's excerpt entry quotes it.)

statements.claim: The hall of Dwaraka fell silent again, heavier than before; the search was over and the waiting had begun.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric close; consistent with the fruitless search just described. No independent factual assertion.

notes: Faithful to HV 1.268 throughout, including the quoted laments and speeches. The messengers' empty-handed return is supported by the pack's excerpt quote ('we saw Aniruddha nowhere'); the passage printout truncates before that point. 'The whole city heard' and the closing gloom are connective.

statements.claim: The search parties returned empty-handed, saying 'We saw Aniruddha nowhere', leaving the Dwaraka assembly without answers.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 excerpt ('we saw Aniruddha nowhere') and corpus-chain continuity with DKS_0328 ('messengers are sent out to search... in vain').

statements.claim: Narada arrived at the assembly and revealed where Aniruddha was and who had taken him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 pack excerpt: 'Nārada... said...' — the report quoted there is the pack's stated evidence for this story (pack index summary: 'Narada arrives at the anxious court and tells Krishna...').

statements.claim: Bana, king of Sonitpura, had a daughter named Usha, and for her sake the Apsara Chitralekha had carried off Aniruddha and brought him to the demon's city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 pack excerpt: '...Vāna... has a daughter by name Ushā. For her, the Apsara Chitralekhā has taken away Kāma's son...' (Aniruddha = son of Pradyumna, who is Kāma incarnate; Vana's city Sonitpura per pack titles).

statements.claim: Bana, learning that Krishna's grandson lay in his city, fettered Aniruddha with serpent-shafts (nooses) and kept him prisoner.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 pack excerpt: 'Vāna... has fettered the highly powerful Aniruddha with serpentine shafts...'

statements.claim: The Yadavas knew Bana's city was ringed with a guardian fire and guarded by his demon armies.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.264: the fire stationed in Vāna's city blazing out to protect him, and the fire-gods' armies (later, in 1.274, 'Vāna's soldiers' and 'great Daitya commanders').

statements.claim: Narada reported that Aniruddha was not deprived of life — bound but alive.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.268 pack excerpt: 'Aniruddha is not still deprived of life.'

statements.claim: Hearing that Aniruddha lived, the weeping wives and the grieving assembly found hope; grief turned toward resolve and Dwaraka toward Sonitpura.
statements.evidence: Psychological bridging to the rescue campaign (evt_0016 arc), not an independent sourceable event.

notes: All core facts (Usha's longing, Chitralekha's abduction, serpent-shaft fetters, Aniruddha alive) come from the pack's 1.268 excerpt entry, which is the pack's stated evidence; the printed passage itself is truncated before Narada's speech, so the excerpt is treated as authoritative. 'Enchantress of the celestial dancers, skilled in the arts of illusion' and the sage's wandering fame are standard descriptive connective.

statements.claim: Rudra/Shiva had come to Bana's aid, fought, and withdrawn from the field before Kartikeya took his place.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274 opening: 'After the high-souled Krishna and Rudra had retired from the battle-field...'; Kottavi later appears 'at the mandate of Mahādeva' to protect Kumāra on the field, confirming Shiva's side against the Yadavas.

statements.claim: Kartikeya, stationed on the chariot brought by Kumbhanda, drove at Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful sharpened arrows; bathed in blood, they fought like three fires.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'Stationed on the car brought by Kumbhānda, Guha (Kārtikeya) drove towards Krishna, Baladeva and Pradyumna and struck them with hundreds of dreadful and sharpened arrows. Bathed in blood those three gods, like unto three fires, fought with Kumara.' ('Kumbhanda the minister' per pack arc/index.)

statements.claim: The Yadus struck Kartikeya with the three weapons given by the Wind-God, Fire-God and Indra; he countered with three weapons of his own, Shaila, Varuna and Savitri; the Yadus, by their illusory powers, devoured every weapon he shot.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: '...struck Kumāra with three weapons given by Wind-God, Fire-God and Indra he, too, with three weapons... namely Shaila, Vāruna and Sāvitri. They however, devoured, by virtue of their illusory powers, all the weapons shot by the great Kumāra.'

statements.claim: Kartikeya, blazing with rage and biting his lips, took up the dreadful Brahmashira weapon, like the Destroyer himself.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'the highly powerful Guha, burning in effulgence and biting his lips, took up the dreadful weapon Brahmashira like unto the Destroyer himself.'

statements.claim: When discharged, the Brahmashira blazed with the effulgence of a thousand suns and was destructive of the world; creatures lost consciousness from its warmth and fled, and the whole universe bewailed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'When the highly dreadful weapon Brahmashira, endued with the effulgence of a thousand suns and destructive of the world, was discharged... the creatures lost their consciousness through its warmth and fled away on all sides and the whole universe bewailed.'

statements.claim: Krishna, the slayer of Keshi, took up his discus, the destroyer and counteractor of all weapons, and as clouds in the rainy season cover the sun's rays, the discus' lustre clouded that of the Brahmashira, which was shorn of its lustre, power and energy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'the powerful Keshava, the slayer of Keshi, took up his discus the destroyer and counteractor of all weapons. As in the rainy season the clouds cover the rays of the sun, so that discus... clouded, with its lustre, that of Brahmashira weapon. When that Brahmashira weapon was shorn of its lustre, power and energy...' ('hung harmless in the sky' is connective.)

statements.claim: Kartikeya, raging like fire fed with clarified butter, seized a dreadful golden Sakti of sure aim, set with bells, glowing like a fire-brand and resembling the fire of dissolution, shouted to strike terror, and discharged it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'Guha... was worked up like fire to which oblation of clarified butter is offered. He then took up a dreadful burning, golden Sakti of sure aim... set with bells, effulgent like a fire-brand and resembling the fire of dissolution. He then set up a powerful shout which struck terror unto his enemies.'

statements.claim: The Sakti rose into the sky, yawned and moved about as if desirous of slaying Krishna; the gods despaired, saying 'Perhaps Krishna will be consumed'; Krishna shouted as if remonstrating and struck it down to the ground, whereupon 'Well done! Well done!' rose from all sides and Indra with the celestials sent up a leonine roar.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'it went up into the sky, yawned and moved about with great force as if desirous of slaying Krishna... Perhaps Krishna will be consumed... shouted and as if remonstrating struck it down on the ground... exclamations "Well done! Well done!" And Vāsava together with the celestials sent up a leonine shout.'

statements.claim: Krishna lifted his discus again, but Kottavi appeared naked at the mandate of Mahadeva to protect Kartikeya, and Lamva, the eighth portion of the goddess, stood between them like a golden spear; Krishna stayed his hand, rebuked her for throwing obstacles in the way of certain destruction, and told her to take Kartikeya and fly from the battlefield, saying it would be well for them if she did, else Kartikeya would fight him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'the beautiful Kottavi, at the mandate of Mahādeva, came there naked for protecting Kumāra. The eighth portion of the goddess, Lamvā, intervened between them like a beautiful golden Sakti... "Oh fie on you? Fly away soon from this place; why do you throw obstacles in the way of certain destruction?"... "Take Guha with you and fly away soon... Or else if I refrain from fighting he will fight with me"... the Lord Hari put away his discus.'

statements.claim: The goddess led Kartikeya from the field and brought him before Shiva (Hara), protected.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'the goddess brought Guha before Hara.'

statements.claim: When Bana saw Guha released from Krishna's discus and retiring from the battle, he felt inclined to fight Madhava himself; his priests performed benedictory ceremonies with mantras, recitation and herbs for victory, and he marched out with dreadful Daitya commanders.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.274: 'When he saw Guha released from Krishna's discus and retire from the battle-field he felt an inclination for fighting himself with Mādhava... chanting the destruction of his enemies his priests... performed benedictory ceremonies... with Mantras, recitation and herbs... Vāna went out with highly dreadful, powerful, energetic and great Daitya commanders.'

statements.claim: Krishna, who had put away his discus rather than strike through a goddess, turned to face the demon king as armies gathered under a darkening sky.
statements.evidence: Closing atmosphere bridging to the Bana duel; Krishna indeed set aside his discus (supported) and Bana now advances to fight him (supported).

notes: Very close paraphrase of HV 1.274 with all named weapons (Brahmashira, Shaila/Varuna/Savitri, the golden Sakti), Kottavi/Lamva episode, and sequence in order. Only additions are atmospheric ('searching for the heart of the one it was meant to kill', 'sky darkened'). No discrepancies with the pack.

statements.claim: The campaign ended with Bana spared and honored with boons; he departed in the company of Rudra.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'Having thus obtained a number of boons Vāna was highly pleased. And having attained to the dignity of Mahākala he went with Rudra.'

statements.claim: Krishna repeatedly asked Narada where Aniruddha lay, his mind overpowered with affection, and Narada answered that the prince was bound with serpents in the female apartment (of Bana's palace).
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'my mind is overpowered with affection. I wish to know truly where Aniruddha is waiting bound with the noose of serpents...' and 'Nārada replied: "O Mādhava, the prince Aniruddha is waiting, bound with serpents, in the female appartment."'

statements.claim: Chitralekha came and told them plainly that this was the female apartment of Bana, king of the Daityas, bidding them enter at ease.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'quickly coming there Chitralekhā said:—O lord, this is the female appartment of the high-souled and energetic king of Daityas Vāna. Do thou enter here at ease.'

statements.claim: Balarama, Krishna, Pradyumna, Narada and Garuda entered the apartment; at the sight of Garuda the huge serpents clinging to Aniruddha's body in the shape of arrows left him at once and dropped to the ground as arrows.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'Baladeva, Krishna, Pradyumna, Narada and Suparna entered into the female appartment... Seeing Garuda, all the huge serpents, which stuck to Aniruddha's person in the shape of arrows, at once left him... dropped on the ground as arrows.'

statements.claim: Aniruddha, delighted, saluted Krishna, bowed to Balarama and to Garuda, and then approached and saluted his father Pradyumna; Usha, encircled by her friends, saluted Krishna and Garuda and bashfully bowed to Pradyumna.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'the noble-minded Aniruddha saluted... Balabhadra. Afterwards... he bowed unto the great Garuda... approached his father Pradyumna and saluted him. Ushā too, encircled by her friends, saluted... Vāshudeva and Suparna... with bashfulness she also bowed unto the holder of the flowery bow (Pradyumna).'

statements.claim: Narada, smiling, showered blessings and hailed Krishna's good fortune at being united with Pradyumna, then asked that a marriage acquired by prowess be celebrated for Aniruddha, saying he desired to see the exchange of jokes between the bridegroom's and bride's parties; all laughed, and Krishna said it would soon be accomplished.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'the highly effulgent Narada smiling... showered blessings on him he said:—O Govinda, by good luck thou hast been united with Pradyumna... celebrate a marriage acquired by prowess for Aniruddha. I have a great desire to see exchange of jokes between the parties of bridegroom and bride. Hearing the words of Nārada all laughed and Krishna said:—O revered Sir, it will soon be accomplished.'

statements.claim: Kumbhanda, Bana's minister who had counselled mercy toward Aniruddha, arrived with all the wedding articles and sought safety from Krishna; Krishna, at Narada's request having already stopped his departure, promised him protection and conferred the kingdom on him, saying he was pleased with his good deeds.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'Kumbhānda, with all the articles for the wedding, arrived... do thou promise me safety... Krishna, at Nārada's request, had already stopped his going... "O Kumbhānda, I have been pleased with hearing of your good deeds. You will now become the king of this kingdom. I confer this kingdom on you. Live you for ever under my protection and be happy and self-controlled with all your kinsmen."' (Minister/mercy counsel per pack index and corpus title.)

statements.claim: Krishna celebrated Aniruddha's wedding, with the Divine Regent of fire present in person; Aniruddha bathed and was adorned, the Apsaras joked with him, the Gandharvas sang auspicious songs, and the Apsaras danced, beautifying the marriage party.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'Janārddana celebrated the wedding festival of Aniruddha. The Divine Regent of fire was present there in person... the Apsaras began to cut diverse jokes with him. The Gandharvas sang melodious and auspicious songs and the Apsaras danced thus beautifying that marriage party.'

statements.claim: Krishna honored Rudra, the giver of boons, and prepared to depart for Dwaraka with the celestials; Kumbhanda told him Bana had cows in Varuna's charge whose nectar-like milk made a man powerful and invincible in battle, and Krishna's mind filled with joy as he set his mind on going there.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'having celebrated Aniruddha's nuptials and honored Rudra, the giver of boons... desired to go away accompanied by the celestials... Vāna has some cows in charge of Varuna. They give nectar-like milk, drinking which a man becomes highly powerful and invincible in battle... Hari's mind was filled with joy. And bent on going there he expressed his desire.'

statements.claim: Brahma blessed Krishna and departed for his own region; Indra and the Maruts set out for Dwaraka; Usha, encircled by her friends, started for Dwaraka too; Balarama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha mounted Garuda's back, and Garuda flew on uprooting trees and shaking the earth.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.276: 'Having blessed Keshava the divine Brahmā departed for his own region... Indra and Maruts... set out for Dwārakā... Ushā, encircled by her friends, started also for Dwārakā. Thereupon Baladeva, Krishna, the highly powerful Pradyumna and energetic Aniruddha sat on Garuda's back. Uprooting the trees and shaking the earth, Garuda, the foremost of birds, went on.'

notes: Faithful to HV 1.276, including the wedding-festival details and Kumbhanda's coronation speech. Recap phrases ('carried off in the night', 'nooses of living serpents', 'enemy king's palace turned wedding hall') match the arc established in DKS_0326-0329 evidence and read as connective narration. Narada 'hailing union with Aniruddha' slightly extends the source's 'united with Pradyumna', but is contextually warranted — not flagged.

statements.claim: Ahuka, his eyes wide with joy, told Krishna that the family rejoiced at his safe return and urged a great festival for Aniruddha's return and wedding; Usha, united with Aniruddha and encircled by her friends, was living in the greatest happiness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'having his eyes expanded with joy the large-armed Ahuka said to the highly effulgent Krishna... seeing thee safely return we are all enjoying... Do thou undertake a great festival for Aniruddha's return and wedding. United with Aniruddha and encircled by her friends the great Ushā is living with the greatest possible pleasure.'

statements.claim: The palace maidens were already celebrating — some playing instruments, some dancing, some singing, some conversing, some playing chess, some wandering about under the influence of wine.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'the damsels of sweet voice are playing on musical instruments in the inner appartment. Some of them are dancing and others are singing. Some with glee are conversing with one another... Some, under the influence of wine, are going to others, and some... are playing at chess.'

statements.claim: Ahuka (relaying Baidarbhi's/Rukmini's view) said the daughter of Kumbhanda should be enlisted as Usha's companion and given to Shamba, the remaining maidens duly given to the other princes, and that festivals should take place in both Krishna's and Aniruddha's residences.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'Baidarbhi says that the great daughter of the high-souled Kumbhānda should be enlisted as Ushā's companion. Confer now that charming and beautiful daughter of Kumbhānda on Shāmva and the remaining maidens should be duly given unto the other princes. Let a great festival take place in thy residence as well as in that of Aniruddha.'

statements.claim: Ahuka's closing words: 'Usha is encircled by her companions; take her into the palace. The noble daughter of Bana is a worthy daughter-in-law of our race. Welcome her with all dignity.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'Ushā is encircled by her companions; take her into the palace. The beautiful and noble daughter of Vāna, by name Ushā, is a worthy daughter-in-law of thy race. Welcome her with all dignity.'

statements.claim: The women of the household, performing benedictory ceremonies as laid down in the ritualistic code, conducted Usha to Aniruddha's house; seeing Aniruddha, Devaki, Revati and Rukmini (the princess of Vidarbha) shed tears of joy.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'females, performing benedictory ceremonies, as laid down in the ritualistic code, conducted the beautiful Ushā to Aniruddha's house. Beholding Aniruddha Devaki, Revati and the Bidarbha princess Rukshmini shed tears of joy.'

statements.claim: As Usha was taken into the room the damsels blew bugles and performed benedictions, and Usha, under the shelter of the Yadu chiefs, lived in the palace enjoying the best of happiness.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'when Ushā was taken into the room, the beautiful damsels, blowing bugles, began to perform benedictory ceremonies. The beautiful Ushā too, under the shelter of the Yadu chiefs, lived in their palace and enjoyed best of happiness.'

statements.claim: After a few days, Chitralekha — the Apsara who had lived among them under the guise of a woman and who had brought Usha and Aniruddha together — departed with the permission of Usha and her companions for the celestial region.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'After a few days, the Apsarā Chitralekha, who was living there under the guise of a woman, with the permission of Ushā and other companions, started for the celestial region.' (Her role in the union is arc continuity from DKS_0329.)

statements.claim: Mayavati, Pradyumna's wife, first invited the Asura princess Usha to her own residence and welcomed her youthful daughter-in-law with costly jewels and dresses; then, by family custom, all the ladies of the Yadu race duly treated the new daughter-in-law.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'after the departure of her companions Māyāvati first invited the beautiful Asura princess Ushā and took her to her own residence. Seeing her youthful and beautiful daughter-in law Ushā Pradyumna's wife welcomed her with costly jewels and dresses. Thereupon according to the custom of the family all the ladies of the Yadu race duly treated the new daughter in-law Ushā.'

statements.claim: Krishna, encircled by the Yadavas and enjoying the highest prosperity, lived on in Dwaraka and governed the whole world, closing the Vana episode.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.277: 'encircled by the Yadavas and enjoying the highest prosperity Krishna lived in Dwarakā and governed the whole world.' (Episode close per pack index.)

statements.claim: The long campaign ended with the enemy spared, the merciful minister rewarded, and a girl from Sonitpura learning to be at home in Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Retrospective summary sentence; each element (Vana spared, Kumbhanda rewarded, Usha welcomed) is individually supported across the pack.

notes: Accurate rendering of HV 1.277, including the specific assignment of Kumbhanda's daughter to Shamba and the Mayavati welcome. One nuance: the source has Ahuka relay Baidarbhi's (Rukmini's) proposal about Kumbhanda's daughter; the story folds this into Ahuka's own speech — the words are still his in the passage, so not flagged. Opening recap ('a prince stolen in the night') is arc connective.

statements.claim: Fearing the prophecy that Devaki's eighth child would kill him, Kamsa ordered his ministers to destroy every embryo of Devaki from the very beginning, to keep her guarded in the inner apartment, and to count the months of every conception from its first day so birth could never take him by surprise.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.57: 'do ye always be on your guard for destroying the (eight born) children of Devaki... from the very beginning destroy all the embryos of Devaki... Let Devaki, well guarded in the inner appartment... count the months from the very first...'; Kamsa's fear of death from Narada's report (1.57 v.8) and of the eighth conception (v.10, 33).

statements.claim: Six children had already been taken from Devaki and killed, one after another, while the guards watched.
statements.evidence: SB 10.2 pack excerpt (rendered: six are killed before the seventh is transferred is the SB arc) and VP 5.1: 'conduct successively six of their princes to be conceived of Devakí'; HV 1.57 has the six Saragarbhas 'born of her womb and proceed to the abode of Death'. (Note: HV 1.57 v.10 loosely says Kamsa will destroy 'the first seven children'; the same passage has only six Saragarbhas placed and the seventh embryo transferred alive — variance noted.)

statements.claim: The six lost children were the Saragarbha princes, sons of the demon Kalanemi, cursed by their own grandfather (Hiranyakasipu) to be born from Devaki and die by Kamsa's hand.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.57: 'Saragarbhas, the sons of Kālanemi... Leaving their own grand-father Hiranyakasipu...' and 'Hiranyakasipu... said... you all six will be born in order from Devaki and Kansa will kill you.'

statements.claim: Vishnu went down to the nether region where the Saragarbhas slept in the waters, entered their dream state, caught their vital breaths and consigned them to the care of Sleep, commanding that they be placed one by one in Devaki's womb so that Kamsa's cruelty would spend itself on them before the real child came.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.57: 'repairing to the nether region Vishnu arrived where Saragarbha Asuras... were living in the womb of water... entering into the body of the Saragarbhas in a state of dream... caught hold of their vital breaths and consigned them to the care of sleep... place them in order in the womb of Devaki... Kansa's efforts will be baffled.'

statements.claim: Vishnu commanded the goddess of sleep, Yogamaya: go to Vraja, the land of cowherds and cattle; draw the embryo called Shesha (Ananta), his elder brother, from Devaki's womb into Rohini's, whereupon he would be known as Sankarshana because he was drawn from one womb to another; when Vishnu's own portion was conceived by Devaki in her eighth pregnancy he would be born as her son.
statements.evidence: SB 10.2.4-15 (Sanskrit): 7th embryo is the vaiṣṇava dhāma 'ananta'; 'gaccha devi vrajaṃ bhadre gopa-gobhir alaṅkṛtam'; 'devakyā jaṭhare garbhaṃ śeṣākhyaṃ dhāma māmakam'; 'garbha-saṅkarṣaṇāt taṃ vai prāhuḥ saṅkarṣaṇaṃ bhuvi'; 'athāham aṃśa-bhāgena devakyāḥ putratāṃ'. HV 1.57: 'take that eldest brother of mine in the seventh month and place him within Rohini's womb... that moon-like elder brother of mine will pass, in his youth, by the name of Sangkarsana.'

statements.claim: Yogamaya herself would be conceived by Yashoda, the most beloved wife of Nanda (master of Kamsa's kine), and born as her daughter; people would worship her under the names Kumuda, Chandika, Krishna, Madhavi and Kanyaka, and Vishnu would make her powerful on earth and adored of all creatures.
statements.evidence: SB 10.2 (Sanskrit v.11-12): 'kumudā caṇḍikā kṛṣṇā mādhavī kanyaketi ca' and worship of her; HV 1.57: 'you will be conceived by Yashodā, the best of milk-women, the most beloved wife of Nanda the master of Kansa's kine'; VP 5.1: 'you shall immediately take a similar character as the embryo offspring of Yaśodá.'

statements.claim: In the seventh month of Devaki's seventh pregnancy the embryo was drawn from her womb into Rohini's, unseen by the watchers; Kamsa believed Devaki had given birth prematurely out of fear, and turned all his vigilance to the eighth conception — never counting the seventh child.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.57: 'when my gentle portion will be conceived by Devaki in her seventh conception, take that eldest brother of mine in the seventh month and place him within Rohini's womb... thinking that Devaki has untimely given birth to a child out of fear in the seventh time Kansa will be very careful for the eighth time when I will be in her womb.'

statements.claim: Rohini's son, the moon-like elder brother, would pass his youth under the name Sankarshana, while in Yashoda's womb the goddess of sleep waited to be born as Nanda's daughter — the girl who would be carried into the prison in a newborn's place.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.57: 'that moon-like elder brother of mine will pass, in his youth, by the name of Sangkarsana... you will be conceived by Yashodā...'; the exchange-night role is the arc's stated design (SB 10.2 rendered excerpt; HV 1.59: the girl is placed on Devaki's bed in exchange for Krishna).

notes: Strongly supported by SB 10.2 (Sanskrit fragments confirm the transfer, Sankarshana etymology, the five names and the aṃśa-bhāgena birth), HV 1.57 and VP 5.1. One source-internal variance: HV 1.57 v.10 says Kamsa will destroy 'the first seven children' while the same passage places only six Saragarbhas and transfers the seventh alive; the story's 'six killed' matches SB/VP and the dominant reading, so no correction needed — noted for the record. 'As quiet as sleep itself' / 'in a single night' are connective.

statements.claim: In the Mathura prison Devaki gave birth to her eighth child, who was the lord himself and withdrew his four-armed form at the terrified request of his father Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.59: 'she conceived him for the eighth time... Devaki gave birth to Vishnu... Vasudeva said to him... do thou withdraw this form of thine... the lord withdrew his form of four arms.'

statements.claim: Vasudeva carried the child through the night to Gokula and returned with the girl just born to Yashoda, wife of the cowherd Nanda — in truth the goddess Yogamaya — laying her on the bed where the eighth child should have been, then announced to Kamsa that a daughter was born.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.59: 'In the same night in which Krishna was born... Yashodā gave birth to her daughter... Vasudeva... speedily repaired to the house of Yashodā. Placing his son in her house... he brought her daughter and placed her on Devaki's bedstead... communicated to... Kansa the birth of a beautiful daughter.' (Goddess identity per SB 10.4.12 'māyā bhagavatī' and pack index.)

statements.claim: Kamsa came at once and demanded the child; Devaki wept, saying 'You have killed my seven sons already. I count this daughter as already slain. Do what you think proper.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.59: 'Kansa quickly arrived at Vasudeva's door... ordered him to hand over the new born babe... Devaki... prayed humbly to him; O lord, you have already killed my seven beautiful sons. I have taken this new-born daughter for already slain. Do what you think proper.'

statements.claim: Kamsa answered that a daughter is killed the moment she is born; seizing her by the feet and whirling her, he dashed her against a stone.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.59: 'While a daughter is born she is already killed... Taking her with contempt by the legs and whirling her Kansa dashed her against a stone.' (SB 10.4.7: 'tāṃ gṛhītvā caraṇayor jāta-mātrāṃ svasuḥ sutām'.)

statements.claim: The girl was not crushed: she sprang from his hands, cast off her mortal form and rose into the sky as a goddess with eight arms, divine garlands and unguents, jewels, a shining crown, unbound hair and dark blue raiment, while Siddhas, Charanas, Gandharvas, Apsaras, Kinnaras and the serpents of the sky surrounded her.
statements.evidence: HV 1.59: 'was not crushed... casting off her human from... adorned with celestial garlands, pastes, and a shining crown she, with dishevelled hairs... rose up in the sky... clad in a dark blue raiment'; SB 10.4.8-10: 'sā tad-dhastāt samutpatya sadyo devy ambaraṃ gatā / divya-srag-ambarālepa-ratnābharaṇa-bhūṣitā / siddha-cāraṇa-gandharvair apsaraḥ-kinnaroragaiḥ'; eight arms per VP 5.3 excerpt and SB pack excerpt.

statements.claim: The goddess told Kamsa: 'What is the use of killing me, fool? The one who will end you is already born.' Then she vanished.
statements.evidence: SB 10.4.11: 'kiṃ mayā hatayā manda jātaḥ khalu tavānta-kṛt' ('What is the use of killing me, fool? Your destroyer is certainly born.'); SB pack excerpt: 'declares, Your slayer is already born elsewhere.' (The story follows SB; HV 1.59's alternate harsher speech — 'I will tear off thy body... drink thy hot blood' — is a variant the pack lists but the SB-based summary treats as the intended reading.)

statements.claim: Kamsa stood amazed and lamented: 'Alas, sister... what have I done in my wickedness. I have abandoned mercy... abandoned kin and friend. Even fate speaks falsely — why should mortals alone be honest?'
statements.evidence: SB 10.4.13-16: 'kaṃsaḥ parama-vismitaḥ... aho bhaginy aho bhāma mayā vāṃ bata pāpmanā / sa tv ahaṃ tyakta-kāruṇyas tyakta-jñāti-suhṛt khalaḥ / daivam apy anṛtaṃ vakti na martyā eva kevalam.'

statements.claim: He told Devaki and Vasudeva not to grieve, that creatures come into the world and leave it and the wise do not divide them into mine and yours, and begged forgiveness of the good who are kind to the fallen.
statements.evidence: SB 10.4.17-22: 'mā śocataṃ mahā-bhāgāv... bhuvi bhaumāni bhūtāni yathā yānty apayānti ca... kṣamadhvaṃ mama daurātmyaṃ sādhavo dīna-vatsalāḥ.'

statements.claim: Kamsa set Devaki and Vasudeva free from their fetters — a thing no one in Mathura had ever seen him do — and Devaki, her anger cooled, answered gently that it was even as he said: embodied beings are driven by grief and joy, fear and hatred, greed, delusion and pride.
statements.evidence: SB 10.4.23-26: 'mocayām āsa nigaḍād viśrabdhaḥ kanyakā-girā / bhrātuḥ samanutaptasya kṣānta-roṣā ca devakī / evam etan mahā-bhāga yathā vadasi dehinām / śoka-harṣa-bhaya-dveṣa-lobha-moha-madānvitāḥ.'

statements.claim: In the prison where six of their children had died, Devaki and Vasudeva stood free; across the river, in Nanda's house, the child she had come to shield slept on.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha (Dutt, Gutenberg #61937) 1.59: Kansa 'killed the Sargarbhas by dashing them against a stone, as soon as they came out' (six Saragarbhas), while Krishna was placed in Yashodā's house in Gokula. ('Across the river' and the morning-after mood are connective.)

notes: Coherently follows the SB 10.4 (7-27) telling that the pack's index names as primary — the gentle 'your slayer is already born' speech, Kamsa's repentance and the release from fetters all match SB. HV 1.59's alternative bloodthirsty girl-speech is a listed variant; the story's choice matches the SB summary (the clearly intended reading per pack index). Devaki's 'seven sons' count is a direct source quote (HV 1.59), and 'six of their children had died' in the prison matches the six Saragarbhas actually dashed there — both internally consistent with the pack. No issues.
